Transcript body:
[00:00] Laura Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. we wanted to focus on the cuda launch failures you've been seeing and put together a concrete playbook, is that right Priya?
[00:12] Priya Nair: Yeah thanks Laura. We've had 2–3 incidents per week where a batch spike during overnight ingestion causes a cascade—cuda launch timeouts, some cublas errors, and then the process gets stuck, sometimes needs a restart. We tried bumping memlimits but it wasn't stable.
[00:29] Marcus Patel: ok, perfect. can you describe the hardware + deployment? on prem, right? are these non-preemptible GPUs?
[00:36] Samir Gupta: Correct, on-prem VPC, 8x A100 per node, driver 525.105 (we think), CUDA 11.8. Some nodes recently had a kernel update; not sure if all nodes matched. We run Redwood Private with the standard mempool.
[00:50] Diego Ramos: quick note — kernel mismatches between driver and host kernel can cause weird launch-time behavior, especially if a page-fault or iommu remap occurs. I've seen similar in other infra teams.
[01:05] Laura Chen: Marcus, can you walk through the typical repro chain we see?
[01:09] Marcus Patel: sure. high-level: under bursty concurrency, we observe memory pressure from two axes: large KV cache sustained by long prefix reuse, and occasional large batches from async ingestion. The runtime's allocator (jemalloc + cuda mempool) fragments over time. When a kernel tries to launch a large matmul it sometimes fails to find a contiguous block, leading to cuda error: launch timeout or CUBLAS_STATUS_ALLOC_FAILED in logs. the reported symptom is sometimes 'CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING timed out' or 'cudaErrorLaunchTimeout'. Logs are noisy, e.g., trace: 'cublasLtMake algorithm: alloc failed -> launch timeout' which is not a single cause.
[01:46] Priya Nair: we've also seen KVCACHE spikes — like a sudden miss storm when a new long prefix gets loaded, evictions cascade and we get spikes in GPU-to-host traffic. Could that aggravate the allocator?
[01:58] Marcus Patel: absolutely. eviction storms cause lots of GPU memcpy churn which temporarily increases transient allocations (pinned host buffers and device staging), which increases fragmentation windows. If a big kernel is scheduled during that window, bad things happen.
[02:12] Rafael Souza: also we did some quantization (int8) for cost reasons — memory usage dropped overall but fragmentation looked worse on long-lived processes. Is that expected?
[02:21] Marcus Patel: yes, quantization changes tensor layouts and sometimes moves allocations around; quantized kernels may use different alloc sizes or workspace patterns which make fragmentation more likely over long runtimes.
[02:31] Ellen Park: are these faults recoverable without restart? we've had to manually restart processes which is painful for our pipelines.
[02:37] Diego Ramos: depends. if the process hits an unrecoverable CUDA context fault you need restart. but many launch-time transient failures can be retried at the request level if we have safe fallback semantics.
[02:48] Laura Chen: ok let's talk retry semantics and safety: what does Redwood recommend?
[02:52] Marcus Patel: our general practice is multi-tier fallback: 1) short exponential retry at request layer (2–3 attempts with jitter) for transient alloc failures; 2) if retries fail, fall back to a smaller model shard or lower batch size (we maintain compatible quantized variants); 3) as a last resort, route to hosted fallback cluster (if SLA allows) or queue the request. For on-prem you can enable per-request failover to other nodes. Important: retries must be idempotent or deduplicated at the app level, because re-sending a generation can produce duplicate side-effects.
[03:26] Priya Nair: our workload triggers a lot of non-idempotent downstream side effects. replays are risky.
[03:31] Marcus Patel: then we use compensating transactions or async ack-ing: accept the request, persist intent, then confirm result. If the inference fails, we mark as failed and run a compensating flow. That pattern avoids double-exec.
[03:41] Samir Gupta: can you be more specific about the mempool? we've got the 'default' redwood cuda mempool config. should we tune it?
[03:49] Diego Ramos: yes. two knobs to try: limit max pool segment size to avoid huge contiguous allocations causing fragmentation; enable periodic pool trimming on low-traffic windows to coalesce free segments; and set a device-side arena to pre-reserve for large kernels so they don't compete with dynamic allocations.
[04:08] Marcus Patel: also enable prefix KV-cache pinning only for hot prefixes, not the whole dataset. aggressive pinning keeps allocated memory high and prevents the allocator from having flexibility.
[04:19] Rafael Souza: what about batch sizing? our ingestion sometimes bursts 200 requests which we batch into 64 per-device. if we lower to 32 we lose throughput but reduce OOMs. any middle ground?
[04:31] Marcus Patel: consider adaptive batching: dynamic batch cap based on free pool size + estimator of upcoming sequence length. The runtime can cap batch sizes during fragmentation windows — we have a config example in the playbook.
[04:44] Priya Nair: can we get concrete thresholds? like if free contiguous memory < X then cap batch to Y?
[04:50] Marcus Patel: yes, a heuristic: if largest_free_block < 1.5 * expected_workspace_for_max_seq then cap batch to floor(largest_free_block / expected_workspace_per_sample). We'll share scripts to estimate.
[05:04] Laura Chen: let's pivot to logs — what should Priya upload for best debug signal?
[05:08] Marcus Patel: please get a) nvidia-smi -q -d MEMORY and MIG if relevant, b) pmap /proc/<pid>/smaps snapshots before/after incident, c) runtime allocator traces (we can enable verbose mempool tracing in Redwood agents), d) full container logs with timestamps, e) kernel dmesg if available. The more correlated traces we have the faster we can root cause.
[05:28] Priya Nair: we can get those. one more oddity: sometimes the cublas errors show mismatched cuBLAS versions between container and host, but our env is supposed to be hermetic.
[05:37] Diego Ramos: common with air-gapped images — drivers on the host vs shipped libcudnn/cublas can misbehave if APIs differ. check nvcc/cuda toolkit versions in container and run 'nvidia-container-cli -k -v' to confirm.
[05:49] Samir Gupta: ok we'll validate versions.
[05:52] Laura Chen: Marcus, can you walk us through a suggested runbook / playbook?
[05:56] Marcus Patel: short version: 1) detection: instrument for 'cuda alloc fail' & 'cublas status alloc failed' patterns and trigger auto-retries and light heap trim; 2) automated mitigations: a) block new large batches for X seconds, b) run pool trim, c) attempt idempotent retry with jitter; 3) escalation: if error rate doesn't drop, drain node from rotation and start diagnostic snapshot; 4) post-mortem: collect allocator traces and run fragmentation analysis to tune pool size and trimming cadence. We'll share a markdown playbook and a sample systemd unit that triggers mempool trim on OOM rates.
[06:33] Priya Nair: does Redwood support kernel fallback — moving to smaller kernels at runtime?
[06:38] Marcus Patel: yes we have a kernel-fallback mechanism: for many ops we support multiple kernel algo families (memory-lean vs speed-lean). If alloc fails for the preferred kernel we can try a memory-saver kernel that uses more compute but less workspace. It's a tradeoff of latency vs reliability. For complicated models we prebuild both kernel paths in the runtime.
[06:56] Rafael Souza: is there an example where fallback causes correctness issues?
[07:00] Diego Ramos: usually not — kernels are algorithmically equivalent. the risk is numerical differences or slightly different output fidelity; so we recommend running a quick eval harness to compare bits for critical prompts.
[07:12] Ellie Park: we need a safe testing plan — we can't risk drifting outputs on prod.
[07:16] Marcus Patel: recommended: run a canary rollout to a small percentage of traffic with the fallback enabled and evaluate prompt fidelity on a held-out promptset (we can help with Redwood's eval harness). if differences are acceptable, enable broader rollout.
[07:30] Priya Nair: what about CUDA_LAUNCH_TIMEOUT specifically — we see 'CUDA_ERROR_LAUNCH_TIMEOUT' in logs, is that hardware scheduling?
[07:37] Marcus Patel: often a watchdog at the driver level fires if kernels exceed the gpu watchdog when running in a shared display context, but on A100s in compute nodes it's usually other causes (hung kernels due to memory allocation stalls or driver deadlock). sometimes the host kernel OOM or PCIe xfer aborts cause the GPU to not respond. Update drivers is important.
[07:57] Samir Gupta: we recently updated to 525.105; should we upgrade to 535.x?
[08:02] Diego Ramos: 535.x has fixes for some nvlink/peer issues; test in staging first. ensure compatible CUDA toolkit in container.
[08:10] Laura Chen: Sofia, we promised a sample docker image for air-gapped fallback testing?
[08:14] Sofia Li: yes, we have a prebuilt image with the fallback kernels and mempool debug enabled. we'll share the sha and a small runbook for enabling it in air-gapped envs.
[08:24] Rafael Souza: about retries — is it safe to retry inside the runtime automatically, or must the app be aware?
[08:30] Marcus Patel: runtime can do safe internal retries for pure inference requests (no side effects). For requests with effects you must either make them idempotent or rely on the app to do retries. Redwood's SDK can be configured to expose retry hooks so the app can choose.
[08:44] Priya Nair: can Redwood throttle incoming client rate to protect allocator health?
[08:48] Marcus Patel: yes, rate-limiters with burst tokens and a dynamic backpressure signal from the mempool are supported. We can cap client concurrency per-tenant and per-node.
[08:58] Samir Gupta: one more instrumentation ask: can you add a metric for largest_free_block_bytes?
[09:03] Marcus Patel: yep, it's on our telemetry road map; we can add it as a custom metric now for Helix.
[09:09] Laura Chen: ok let's do a quick live debugging segment — Priya, can you share the last incident log?
[09:14] Priya Nair: I pasted it in the chat. it's blunt, apologies if messy.
[09:18] [screen-share / log paste sounds]
[09:20] Marcus Patel: reading... here's a snippet we often see: 'E 2026-06-12T05:12:34Z runtime: cublasLt matmul: CUBLAS_STATUS_ALLOC_FAILED; fallback make algo mem alloc failed; then cudaErrorLaunchTimeout' — that pattern indicates an alloc fail followed by attempted fallback algos then a timer firing.
[09:38] Diego Ramos: there's also a kernel OOM trace in the dmesg: 'NVRM: Xid 86: GPU at fault: page fault' — Xid 86 historically correlates to illegal memory access or corrupted pointers in kernels, but combined with alloc failures it's often fragmentation.
[09:54] Priya Nair: interesting, ok.
[09:57] Laura Chen: we should capture a pmap/smaps before and after next incident — maybe the allocator grows RSS in weird ways.
[10:04] Marcus Patel: agreed. Diego, can you summarize recommended immediate config changes for Helix?
[10:08] Diego Ramos: immediate steps: 1) enable mempool trimming every 30 minutes during low load, 2) reduce KV-cache pin threshold to top-500 prefixes only, 3) enable adaptive batching with conservative caps, 4) deploy fallback kernels image to canary nodes, 5) run driver/toolkit version validation and upgrade in staging to 535.x where possible.
[10:28] Priya Nair: good. how long to see impact?
[10:31] Marcus Patel: you should see fewer incidents within 24–72 hours after trimming + adaptive batching; fallback kernels reduce severity immediately on canary.
[10:39] Laura Chen: wrapping up — we'll send the playbook, the sample container, and a short checklist for incident capture. any other open Qs?
[10:47] Ellen Park: timeline wise — can Redwood run a bench next week with our workload?
[10:51] Laura Chen: yes let's schedule a 1-hr bench during your low-traffic window; Marcus will coordinate.
[10:56] Priya Nair: thanks all.
[10:58] Laura Chen: thanks team, we'll follow up with the artifacts.
